name: Classical Athens
title: Social Hierarchy of Classical Athens: From Rich Citizens to Enslaved
period: 508–322 BCE (from the reforms of Cleisthenes to the end of the democracy)

tiers.name: Richest citizens
tiers.you: Your estates yield more than 500 measures a year; you may be called on to fit out a warship or pay for a chorus, and you can serve as a treasurer of Athena, but the Assembly can still vote you into exile.
tiers.kid: The richest Athenians were expected to pay for warships and for the plays at the city’s festivals.
tiers.rise: Membership depended on wealth, not birth: a family rose into the class as its fortune grew and fell out of it when the fortune was lost, while ostracism sent a leading man into exile for ten years without taking his property.
tiers.why: At the top stood the pentakosiomedimnoi, the “five-hundred-measure men”, whose land yielded at least 500 medimnoi of grain, oil or wine a year; Solon had defined the class in 594 BCE by wealth rather than birth.

tiers.name: Knights
tiers.you: Your land yields more than 300 measures a year, enough to keep a horse; you ride in the city’s cavalry, drill in peacetime and parade in the great festival processions.
tiers.kid: Knights were rich Athenians who could afford a horse and rode in the city’s cavalry.
tiers.rise: Membership followed income, not birth: a family entered the class when its land yielded 300 measures and left it when its fortune shrank.
tiers.why: The hippeis, or knights, were the second class: men whose land yielded at least 300 medimnoi a year, enough, in Aristotle’s account, to keep a horse.

tiers.name: Hoplite class
tiers.you: You farm your own land in the Attic countryside, pay for your own shield and spear, and stand shoulder to shoulder in the phalanx when the city goes to war.
tiers.kid: Farmers of the hoplite class bought their own shields and spears and fought side by side.
tiers.rise: Membership followed the yield of a man’s land, so a poorer citizen who prospered could rise into the class, and a farmer ruined by debt or war could sink out of it.
tiers.why: The zeugitai were the citizens whose land yielded at least 200 medimnoi a year.

tiers.name: Poorer citizens
tiers.you: You work a small plot or sell your labour in the city; you vote in the Assembly, may sit on a jury for three obols a day, and row in the fleet when Athens goes to war.
tiers.kid: Poorer citizen men could vote in the Assembly, serve on juries and row the city’s warships.
tiers.rise: A poorer citizen whose farm or trade prospered could rise into the hoplite class; after the defeat in the Lamian War in 322 BCE, at least 12,000 poorer citizens were stripped of their citizenship.
tiers.why: The thetes were the citizens whose land yielded less than 200 medimnoi a year, or who had none: smallholders, craftsmen, shopkeepers and labourers in the city and the port of Piraeus.

tiers.name: Metics
tiers.you: You are free to live, work and trade in Athens, but you pay the metic tax, need a citizen to sponsor you, and can never vote or own the house you live in.
tiers.kid: Metics were free people from other places who lived and worked in Athens but could not vote.
tiers.rise: Citizenship was granted only rarely, by a special vote of the Assembly, as it was to the freed slave and banker Pasion; in 404 BCE the Thirty Tyrants seized the property of rich metics and put Lysias’s brother Polemarchus to death.
tiers.why: Metics were free people who lived in Athens without being citizens: Greeks from other cities drawn by its trade and wealth, some non-Greeks, and freed slaves.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were bought from a slave trader; you work beside your owner on a farm or in a workshop, but you can be sold or beaten, and in court your word counts only under torture.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; some were later freed.
tiers.rise: Owners could free their slaves, often in return for the slave’s own savings, and a freed slave became a metic with duties to the former owner; the slaves who rowed at the Battle of Arginusae in 406 BCE were freed and may have been made citizens.
tiers.why: Slaves did much of the work of Attica.
